name: Nishida Shuzoten (Den, all-junmai brewery, Aomori)
text: Brewery founded in 1878 (Meiji 11) and described as the only sake brewery within Aomori City. It is best known for the brand Den (田酒) and for committing to an all-junmai line-up.
flavor: Flavor profile is not described in the sources consulted; judge by tasting the junmai range.
use: Served as junmai sake, warm or chilled according to the particular bottling; listed among Aomori's top-ranked sake in consumer rankings.
craft: The distinguishing point for a buyer is the all-junmai policy: no brewer's alcohol is added anywhere in the range, so spec sheets can be read on rice and polishing ratio alone. Specific rice and yeast details were not in the search results.

name: Hachinohe Shuzo (Mutsu Hassen, Hachinohe)
text: Aomori brewery recorded as founded in 1775, which makes it one of the older houses in the prefecture. Its main brand is Mutsu Hassen (陸奥八仙).
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Sold as the Mutsu Hassen range; appears in Aomori sake rankings.
craft: Founding year is taken from a ranking-site summary, not from the brewery's own page; confirm with the maker before quoting it in print.

name: Asabiraki (Morioka brewery)
text: Sake brewery in Morioka, Iwate, founded in 1871 (Meiji 4). It is listed among the long-established houses of the prefecture.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Regional sake sold under the Asabiraki name; found in Iwate sake rankings.
craft: Only the founding year and city are supported by the results seen; brewing specifics (rice, yeast, polishing ratios) were not available and are left out.

name: Shiba Shuzoten (Hiroki)
text: Iwate sake brewery founded in 1903 (Meiji 36). Its main brand is Hiroki (廣喜).
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Sold regionally as Hiroki; appears in Iwate rankings.
craft: Information was limited to founding year and brand name; no process details were found, so none are given.

name: Niizawa Jozoten (Hakurakusei)
text: Miyagi sake brewery founded in 1873. It is known for the brand Hakurakusei (伯楽星).
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Sold as Hakurakusei; listed in Miyagi sake rankings.
craft: The results supported only the founding year and flagship brand. Check the maker's own site for the rice, polishing and yeast specifics before specifying it on a menu.

name: Saura (Urakasumi)
text: Miyagi brewery with a history described as close to 300 years. Its main brand is Urakasumi (浦霞), one of the best-known sake names of the prefecture.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Urakasumi is sold widely as a Miyagi regional sake and is common on izakaya and sushi menus.
craft: The exact founding year was not given in the results seen; only the approximate span of nearly 300 years. Do not quote a specific year without checking the maker.

name: Uchigasaki Shuzoten (Miyagi)
text: Miyagi sake brewery whose founding is given as 1661 (Kanbun 1), which places it among the oldest houses of the prefecture.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Regional sake; of interest mainly for its age.
craft: The founding date comes from a single ranking summary and is stated there as 'among the oldest'. Verify with the brewery before citing it as the oldest.

name: Hiraiko Shuzo (Hidakami)
text: Miyagi brewery that makes Hidakami (日高見). Sources disagree on its founding: one gives 1861 (Bunkyu 1), another 1902 (Meiji 35).
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Sold as Hidakami; appears in Miyagi sake rankings.
craft: Because the two founding years differ by about forty years, treat both as unconfirmed until the brewery's own history page is checked. This is a good example of why founding years on aggregator sites should be cross-checked.

name: Kokki Shuzo (Mashike, northernmost brewery)
text: Brewery in Mashike, Hokkaido, founded in 1882 (Meiji 15) during the herring boom. It is described as Japan's northernmost sake brewery and ships about 4,000 koku. A Hokkaido government page says it began to make sake to warm fishermen working in cold seas.
flavor: Soft dry (yawarakai karakuchi) according to the source.
use: Regional sake; served to match Hokkaido seafood.
craft: Brewing water is snowmelt from the Shokanbetsu mountain range. The 4,000-koku figure is from a retailer column and may change; the founding year is Meiji 15 in all results seen.

name: Otokoyama (Asahikawa)
text: Asahikawa sake maker with a founding year given as 1887 (Meiji 20). The name Otokoyama is said to originate in Itami in the Kanbun era, about 300 years ago, and the Asahikawa house is described as having taken it over from the Yamamoto family of Kinuwataya in 1968. In 1977 it is said to have won a gold medal at Monde Selection, the first for Japanese sake.
flavor: Dry and clean (karakuchi tanrei) per the sources.
use: Served as a regional dry sake; a visitor-oriented brewery.
craft: Brewing water is subsoil water seeping from the permanent snow of the Daisetsuzan range. The sources give two different origin stories (Meiji 20 versus Itami in the 1600s), so quote the Asahikawa house's founding as 1887 only with the caveat that the brand name predates it.

name: Aizu Shuzo (Minamiaizu)
text: Brewery in Minamiaizu (former Tajima), southwest Fukushima near the Tochigi border, said to have been founded in 1688. One source gives the era only as Genroku. The family is said to have made miso and shoyu at its main house before building a dedicated sake brewery.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Regional sake from the Minamiaizu area.
craft: Two sources differ in precision (1688 versus the Genroku era), which is consistent but not identical. The miso-and-shoyu prehistory is a useful reminder that many Tohoku sake houses grew out of general fermentation businesses.

name: Tsurunoe Shuzo (Aizuwakamatsu)
text: Aizuwakamatsu brewery that began as a branch house in Kansei 6 (1794) under the trade name Eihoya (永宝屋). It is described as descending from a family that served as purveyor to the Aizu domain.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Aizu regional sake.
craft: Only the history is supported by the results. The Kansei 6 date refers to the branch founding, not the original family business.

name: Suehiro Shuzo (Aizuwakamatsu)
text: Aizuwakamatsu brewery founded in Kaei 3 (1850). It is described as one of the larger houses in the Aizu area, in both output and range of products.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Wide-range Aizu sake maker; suitable as a regional reference brewery.
craft: The scale comparison ('large for Aizu') comes from a Wikipedia summary and is relative; no figures were in the results.

name: Takahashi Shosaku Shuzoten (Aizuwakamatsu)
text: Aizuwakamatsu brewery said to date from about 1875. It follows a principle of 'dosan dohou' (土産土法), brewing with local rice and water by local methods.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Aizu local sake.
craft: The founding date is given as approximate ('around 1875'). The local-rice, local-water principle is a stated policy of the house rather than a certified standard.

name: Sasamasamune Shuzo (Kitakata)
text: Kitakata brewery founded in Bunsei 1 (1818). It is described as one of the first in Japan to make and sell pure rice sake (junmaishu) and as a trigger of the jizake boom.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Kitakata regional sake.
craft: The 'early junmai' and 'jizake boom' claims are the brewery's reputation as summarised by a Fukushima brewery guide; treat them as attribution, not an audited first.

name: Takagi Shuzo (Juyondai, Murayama)
text: Brewery in Tominami, Murayama City, Yamagata, a heavy-snow area. Founded in 1615 (Genna 1); the head takes the name Tatsugoro in each generation and the present head is the 15th. The old main brand was Asahitaka (朝日鷹). The 15th head created Juyondai (十四代) in 1994 in his mid-twenties.
flavor: Juyondai is known for a rich, sweet-umami style (houjun umakuchi).
use: Premium sake, extremely hard to buy; the ranking pages list tiers of Juyondai bottlings.
craft: The brand name comes from the 14th head's era, when a trademark containing a number was accepted; accounts vary on details of that story. Asahitaka remains the local everyday label.

name: Ishimago Honten (Yuzawa)
text: Shoyu and miso brewer in the Iwasaki district of Yuzawa, Akita, founded in Ansei 2 (1855). It uses only Akita rice, soybeans and wheat, with natural fermentation. Shoyu is made in huge wooden barrels about four metres around the waist, kept in a building that is a nationally registered cultural property.
flavor: Hand-made natural-fermentation character; no tasting notes in the sources.
use: Table shoyu (for example the Hyakuju line) and miso for Akita home cooking and restaurants.
craft: Moving the barrels and stirring the moromi are done by hand. Shoyu and miso have separate buildings. Check the vintage and barrel age of the Hyakuju label with the maker.

name: Ando Jozo (Kakunodate)
text: Miso, shoyu and pickle maker in Kakunodate, Semboku, Akita, founded in Kaei 6 (1853). Its main shop has a brick-built storehouse room from the mid-Meiji period. It stresses additive-free, naturally brewed seasonings.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Miso, shoyu and pickles sold through its own shops and mail order.
craft: The maker advertises additive-free and natural brewing; the sources did not state barrel type or fermentation length.

name: Sato Yosuke Shoten (Inaniwa udon, Yuzawa)
text: Inaniwa udon maker in Yuzawa, Akita, whose founding is dated 1860 (Manen 1), when Inaniwa Kichizaemon passed the technique to his fourth son Sato Yosuke to avoid the line dying out. The craft was kept as a one-heir-only secret until it was opened up (one source says Showa 47) and the firm was incorporated in Showa 55.
flavor: Not described in detail; a visitor account praises the throat feel.
use: Hand-pulled dried udon eaten cold or hot.
craft: Origin dates conflict: 1665 (Kanbun 5) is cited for Inaniwa Kichizaemon or for Sato Ichibei of Ozawa, and a third view places Kichizaemon's dried udon from about 1736. The 1860 date is only for this shop. The name Yosuke is inherited; the present head is the eighth.

name: Sasacho Jozo (Hanamaki)
text: Shoyu and miso brewer in Hanamaki, Iwate, founded in Meiji 39 (1906). Wooden barrels still stand in the shoyu hall and the moromi is stirred by hand, not by machine.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Shoyu and miso for local use and sale through shoyu specialist retailers.
craft: Wooden barrels with hand stirring are the points to ask about; barrel age and koji ratio were not in the results.

name: Yagisawa Shoten (Rikuzentakata)
text: Shoyu, miso and koji-amazake maker founded in 1807 (Bunka 4) in Rikuzentakata, Iwate. The 2011 earthquake and tsunami swept the brewery away, and shipping of shoyu resumed in 2013 from Ichinoseki.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Shoyu, miso and koji amazake sold via its online shop.
craft: Rebuilding a brewery after the loss of the building and barrels is the notable point of this house's recent history; ask the maker which line comes from which site.

name: Daikoku Shoyu (Karumai)
text: Shoyu and miso maker in Karumai, Iwate, with a history of about 100 years. It makes koji on covered trays (futa-koji) and presses shoyu in the old fune-style press, with maturing in large wooden vats.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Shoyu, miso, and perilla-leaf wrapped miso (egoma shiso-maki miso).
craft: Tray koji (futa-koji) allows better control of temperature and moisture in small batches; pressing in the traditional way is a labour-intensive finish. Both are stated by the maker.

name: Shoyura Suzuki (Suzuki Shoyuten, Tenei)
text: Small shoyu house in Tenei village, Fukushima, more than 130 years old. Its brewery has just ten wooden barrels and a koji room.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Shoyu for direct sale and for restaurants seeking small-batch product.
craft: Ten barrels set a ceiling on yearly output, so check supply before committing to it for volume use.

name: Soma Yamabun Yamagataya (Soma)
text: Miso and shoyu brewer in Soma, Fukushima, which states on its site that it has operated for 150 years.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Miso and shoyu for local and mail-order sale.
craft: The 150-year figure is the maker's own claim; no exact founding year was given in the search results.

name: Washida Tamizo Shoten (Tsuruoka)
text: Koji, miso, shoyu and amazake maker in Tsuruoka, Yamagata, producing since the Meiji era. It makes rice koji from Shonai-grown rice only.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Koji, miso, shoyu and amazake.
craft: Using single-origin Shonai rice for koji is a stated point; an exact founding year was not found.

name: Shoji Kunizo Shoten (Yamagata Maruyama Shoyu)
text: Shoyu brewer in Yamagata City, founded in 1946 and known as Yamagata Maruyama Shoyu. It also makes aji-tamari and tamari-su (tamari vinegar).
flavor: Tamari-type products would be expected to be rich, but this is not stated in the sources.
use: Shoyu, tamari-style seasoning and tamari vinegar.
craft: A postwar house, unlike most entries here. The tamari vinegar is an unusual product worth asking about.

name: Yamaki Jozo (Ryozen, Date)
text: Miso and shoyu brewery at the foot of Mount Ryozen in Date, Fukushima, which began around 1945, at the end of the war.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Miso and shoyu.
craft: Postwar founding; only the origin and place were supported by the results.

name: Kashiwaya (Usukawa manju, Fukushima)
text: Confectioner founded in 1852, known for the usukawa manju (thin-skin bean-jam bun), said to be the root of thin-skin manju elsewhere and counted as one of Japan's three great manju.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted; the product is defined by its thin skin.
use: Gift sweet and tea-time wagashi.
craft: The 'three great manju' ranking is a popular list, not an official one. Skin thinness and bean paste texture are the points to judge.

name: Kuju Honpo Tamazawa (Shimobashira)
text: Miyagi confectioner founded in 1675, known for Shimobashira (霜ばしら), a candy that can only be made in winter and is sold from October to April.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Seasonal candy sold as a gift sweet.
craft: Production is limited to the cold season because of the process; the sources do not say why in detail.

name: Urokoya Sohonten (Yamagata)
text: Yamagata confectioner that states its founding as 1684. It makes both wagashi and Western-style confectionery.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Wagashi and yogashi for local gifting.
craft: The 1684 date is from the shop's own heading; product specifics were not in the results.

name: Choeido (Yamagata)
text: Yamagata confectioner with more than 130 years of history over five generations. It makes fukimame (富貴豆) and noshi-ume.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Traditional Yamagata sweets, sold as gifts and with tea.
craft: Fukimame and noshi-ume are the signature items; the sources give no process detail.

name: Kimuraya (Koukyou, Tsuruoka)
text: Tsuruoka confectioner founded in 1887. Its famous sweet Kokyo (古鏡) is named for an old mirror unearthed from the Kagami-ike pond on Haguro-san, one of the Three Mountains of Dewa.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Yamagata gift sweet.
craft: The name is a local-history link; the recipe was not described in the results.

name: Noshiume Honpo Satoya (Yamagata)
ja: 乃し梅本舗 佐藤屋
text: Yamagata confectioner trading since the Edo period and making noshi-ume, a sheet confection of ume. Its site claims two hundred years of history.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Gift sweet.
craft: No process details or exact founding year were found in the results; the 200-year claim is the shop's own.

name: Kajiwara Konbu-ten (Hakodate)
text: Kelp specialist in Hakodate with shops including one at the Hakodate morning market. The heading gives its founding as Showa 47 (1972). Its oboro kombu is shaved thinly by craftsmen.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Oboro kombu and kombu for dashi.
craft: The general process for oboro or tororo kombu is to layer vinegar-soaked dried kombu and shave the side of the block into thin sheets. Hakodate's coast is the main source of mako-kombu, noted for refined sweetness.

name: Saikichi Shoten (Kesennuma sanma-bushi)
text: Kesennuma maker of sanma-bushi (dried smoked saury) dashi products. The saury is processed by Hiwatari Suisan, and a source says Konno, counted by generations, is at least the 18th.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Sanma-bushi dashi and tsuyu for professional kitchens.
craft: Sanma-bushi is an alternative to katsuobushi for dashi; a professional should test it for oiliness and smoke in a clear broth. The generation count is the source's own and loosely worded.
